                                      PROJECT NO. 58000
 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                            §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                        §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY                      §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION                             §                     OF TEXAS

     OCCIDENTAL CHEMICAL CORPORATION’S COMMENTS TO PROPOSED
           AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 AND §25.193 AND NEW §25.252

                                      I.    INTRODUCTION

       Occidental Chemical Corporation (OxyChem) appreciates the opportunity to submit these

comments to express its serious concerns with the proposed changes to the Commission’s

transmission cost allocation policies and to recommend that the Commission adopt narrow,

specific exceptions to any new cost allocation methodology to account for the operational and

business realities that face legacy industrial sites that are co-located with dispatchable qualifying

cogeneration facilities (collectively, “legacy cogeneration facilities”).       Specifically, if the

Commission departs from its existing 4CP transmission cost allocation methodology, it should

grandfather legacy cogeneration facilities from that change and continue to allocate transmission

charges to the loads at those sites based on their usage during ERCOT’s summer 4CP.

Alternatively, if the Commission wishes to adopt a more targeted exemption, it should at least

ensure that legacy cogeneration facilities are not assigned transmission costs based on their usage

during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December), when the

transmission system has ample capacity and cogeneration is generally taken offline for prudent

preventative maintenance. Special consideration is warranted for legacy cogeneration facilities

like OxyChem’s, which were financed and constructed decades ago under prior regulatory

constructs that focused transmission cost allocation on usage during the summer peaks. As

described below, a 12CP system would disproportionately penalize legacy cogeneration facilities



                                                 1
 for performing operationally prudent maintenance during the spring and fall, would diminish

economic incentives to prioritize the reliable operation of their cogeneration, and could severely

impact their continued economic viability, to the detriment of all rate classes, including

residentials, and the ERCOT grid overall.

        OxyChem operates seven large chemical plants across the ERCOT region that, as of July

2026, collectively employ over 1,500 Texans. 1 Reliable and cost-effective electricity is a critical

operational input to OxyChem’s manufacturing operations and a key factor influencing the global

competitiveness and long-term viability of its facilities. At OxyChem’s two largest Texas plants,

electricity is a critical raw material and represents one of the largest components of operating costs.

Those two facilities are co-located and operationally integrated with cogeneration units that

provide, steam, waste heat, and electricity for integrated manufacturing operations. Importantly,

because OxyChem’s cogeneration provides essential power and steam to its manufacturing plants,

OxyChem is strongly incentivized to keep those generators running around the clock, with a focus

on high reliability, especially at times when generation reserves are low on the grid and procuring

replacement power would be especially expensive. This cogeneration structure not only benefits

OxyChem by allowing it to meet a significant share of its manufacturing plants’ electricity needs

throughout the year, it also results in operational efficiencies that reduce demand on the grid.

Additionally, the reliability and availability of OxyChem’s thermal, dispatchable cogeneration also

directly contributes to system stability and resource adequacy because those sites have the

flexibility to reduce their co-located load in order to increase exports, which provides additional

dispatchable capacity on the grid at critical times.


         1
            As of July 2026, OxyChem’s seven manufacturing facilities employ 1,049 direct employees and 482
contractors. Those numbers do not include corporate positions that support the manufacturing plants, nor the
additional contractors who are employed on an ad hoc basis for specific projects or plant turnarounds.

                                                     2
        OxyChem strongly supports retaining ERCOT’s current four summer coincident peak

(4CP) allocation methodology. The Commission’s current 4CP system is appropriately rooted in

cost causation principles because it assigns transmission costs to customers based on their

contribution to ERCOT’s system peaks, and the need to reliably serve peak demand is what

actually drives the need for most new transmission investment.              Further, 4CP allocation

appropriately aligns customers’ incentives with the needs of the ERCOT grid. This is especially

true of industrial facilities, like OxyChem’s largest facilities, that are integrated with cogeneration

and have a much different impact on the ERCOT grid than loads that are entirely served from the

ERCOT transmission system. The Commission’s current transmission cost allocation rules

provide legacy cogeneration facilities with strong price signals to ensure that cogeneration units

are operating at their full capacity across each of the 4CPs, because that will mitigate the coincident

peak transmission charges that the co-located loads are assigned in the coming year. Even outside

of the 4CP, OxyChem keeps its cogeneration units up and running across most hours of the year,

which minimizes its net demand on the ERCOT system across far more than just the peak intervals.

That said, like any generation facilities, OxyChem’s cogeneration units cannot stay online

indefinitely. Under the current transmission cost allocation system, OxyChem is appropriately

incentivized to time its cogeneration maintenance activities (and other operational events that

result in more of OxyChem’s demand being placed on the grid) during the spring (March, April,

May) and fall (October, November, December) when demand on the ERCOT grid is at its lowest.

From a policy perspective, it makes sense to encourage planned generation maintenance in the

spring and fall because that results in some or all of the co-located load being served by the grid

at times when additional demand does not contribute to ERCOT’s annual system peak or cause

ERCOT utilities to incur additional costs to expand the transmission system.



                                                  3
        In contrast, under a 12CP system, customers would incur transmission charges based on

their demand during the peak interval in every month, regardless of whether that peak interval has

any bearing on the need for more transmission. Shifting to a 12CP transmission cost allocation

scheme would interfere with customers’ incentives to minimize their demand on the ERCOT grid

across the most critical intervals for both reliability and system costs. Providing customers with

signals to manage their usage during low-demand months does not create any reliability benefits

and does not conform with cost-causation principles. Instead, 12CP allocation simply serves to

shift costs onto higher load factor industrial customers, including some, like OxyChem, whose

contributions to ERCOT’s monthly CPs are at their greatest when overall demand on the system

is at its lowest, something the Commission should seek to protect and actively encourage.

Specifically, a 12CP system would unfairly penalize facilities like OxyChem’s by saddling them

with transmission charges for placing additional demand on the grid when they engage in

necessary and operationally prudent cogeneration maintenance, even if they efficiently arrange

their maintenance intervals in low-demand months when the outages will have the least possible

impact on the broader grid.

       However, in the event the Commission decides to shift transmission cost allocation in

ERCOT to a 12CP system, OxyChem strongly recommends that the Commission create an

exemption that will grandfather and allow a small set of legacy cogeneration facilities to continue

to be billed under the current 4CP construct. As discussed above, the current 4CP system

appropriately incentivizes reductions in grid usage during the four summer peaks, which has

reliability benefits and diminishes the need for future transmission investment. Additionally,

retaining a 4CP methodology for a limited set of legacy cogeneration facilities will preserve those

facilities’ strong financial incentives to ensure that their cogeneration is online and fully


                                                4
 operational during ERCOT’s highest system peaks so that it can offset the demand of the co-

located load and provide any excess capacity onto the ERCOT grid, as well as those sites’

incentives to schedule cogeneration maintenance during the spring and fall (March-May and

October-December) when the reliability of the ERCOT grid is not in question, and when the drivers

for new transmission investment are not present. In contrast, incentivizing demand reductions

during off-peak months has no corresponding system benefit, and may actually harm reliability by

causing load reductions when the system lacks sufficient inertia on the supply side. Further,

retaining the current 4CP allocation methodology will preserve the economics of legacy

cogeneration facilities, many of which were financed and built under prior regulatory constructs,

including those that pre-date market open, which all had a strong 4CP element to reflect the

realities of the ERCOT system. Moving away from this long-standing policy could jeopardize the

ability of legacy cogeneration facilities (not just OxyChem’s, but also those of other industrial

companies engaged in energy intensive industries) to maintain profitability and continue operating

at their current scale. This is because legacy cogeneration facilities that typically only use the

ERCOT transmission system as a backup source of supply would be forced to begin paying

significant transmission charges—not because of any operational characteristics that put strain on

the ERCOT grid or cause the need for new transmission investment, but simply because they chose

to engage in prudent and necessary cogeneration maintenance practices that not only benefit their

operators, but the broader ERCOT grid. Such a result would be exceedingly poor public policy.

       Alternatively, if the Commission wishes to apply an updated allocation methodology (such

as 12CP) to legacy cogeneration facilities, the Commission should create a targeted exemption

process that would at least allow those facilities to avoid incurring transmission charges based on

their net demand during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December).


                                                5
 Such an exemption or “safe harbor” would encourage legacy cogeneration facilities to engage in

operationally prudent generation maintenance at times when taking their generation offline poses

the least possible reliability risk and least cost impact, while still incentivizing them to keep that

generation online and fully operational to offset their exposure to transmission charges during the

remainder of the year. In contrast, if those facilities are subjected to a 12CP cost allocation

methodology without any exemption, that would expose them to significant transmission cost

exposure whenever their generation is shut down or derated—irrespective of whether that occurs

during times of system stress. Additionally, requiring facilities to alter cogeneration or industrial

operations to avoid 12CP exposure could create inefficient and potentially counterproductive

operating incentives, and could ultimately result in more of those facilities’ load being served by

the ERCOT grid during periods when reliability is most in question, something that is contrary to

the Commission’s objective of ensuring system reliability. Importantly, imposing economic

disincentives on prudently maintaining and efficiently operating legacy cogeneration facilities

would hurt ratepayers across all customer classes, including residential customers, by increasing

costs and placing additional strain on the grid.

       As described below, if the Commission chooses to depart from its traditional 4CP

transmission cost allocation methodology, it could easily establish a narrow, administrable

exemption process that would only apply to a relatively small number of legacy cogeneration

facilities. Notably, while OxyChem believes that such an exemption is justified based on the

operational characteristics and incentives of those legacy cogeneration facilities, OxyChem is not

suggesting that those are the only types of customers that are deserving of additional consideration

or grandfathering in the Commission’s rules.




                                                   6
                                 II.   GENERAL COMMENTS

   A. The Commission should retain the existing 4CP transmission cost allocation
      methodology, either generally across ERCOT or specifically for legacy cogeneration
      facilities.
       As explained above, the Commission’s current 4CP transmission cost allocation

methodology is appropriately rooted in cost causation principles and should be retained. The need

to reliably serve peak demand is what actually drives the need for new transmission investment,

and the 4CP construct assigns transmission costs to customers based on their contributions to the

four system peaks that occur during the summer months, when overall demand on the ERCOT

grid is at its highest. Just as importantly, the current methodology aligns customers’ incentives

with the needs of the ERCOT grid. Because customers can reduce their transmission charges by

minimizing their demand during the 4CP intervals, the current system rewards behavior—like

keeping co-located cogeneration online and fully operational across the summer peaks—that

provides real reliability benefits and diminishes the need for future transmission investment. In

other words, reductions in grid usage during the four summer peaks have an offsetting benefit to

the grid, which is precisely the type of cost-causative relationship that should underlie any

transmission cost allocation methodology.

       However, if the Commission decides to abandon the 4CP system, given the unique

characteristics of legacy cogeneration facilities like OxyChem’s, it would be prudent and fair for

the Commission to grandfather those facilities and allow them to continue to be billed based on

the 4CP methodology. At industrial cogeneration sites, industrial electrical load, steam demand,

process operations, and cogeneration output are operationally interconnected. Generation dispatch

decisions at those sites must prioritize safe, reliable, and efficient operation of continuous

industrial processes, including steam balance, process heat requirements, equipment constraints,

emissions compliance, and worker safety.      Unlike stand-alone loads, cogeneration facilities

                                                7
 generally cannot treat electric load reduction as a simple economic response without potentially

disrupting production, process safety, product quality, contractual commitments, or steam system

reliability. As such, load curtailment solely to mitigate coincident peak transmission charges is

not a primary operational objective for legacy cogeneration facilities. The Commission should

avoid a cost allocation structure that encourages those facilities to make operational decisions

based primarily on poor transmission billing signals rather than safe, reliable, efficient, and

environmentally responsible integrated operations.

        These operational realities also demonstrate why a 12CP methodology would be

particularly inappropriate for legacy cogeneration facilities. A methodology based on a broader

set of monthly system peaks would subject those facilities to transmission cost exposure during

periods when operationally prudent generation maintenance or process conditions limit their

ability to optimize their net load. And, during the spring and fall, managing usage during

ERCOT’s monthly peak intervals provides no offsetting benefit to the grid—it simply shifts costs

to industrial customers without any corresponding cost-causative rationale.         In contrast, as

discussed above, reducing demand on the grid during the four summer peak intervals does provide

an offsetting benefit, because those are the intervals that drive the need for new transmission

investment and present the greatest risk to the reliability of the ERCOT grid. Further, diluting the

impact of the summer 4CP will decrease legacy cogeneration facilities’ incentives to ensure that

their thermal, dispatchable generation is maximally available at the most critical times for grid

stability and reliability.

        Finally, the Commission should recognize that legacy cogeneration facilities were

developed under a materially different regulatory and cost allocation framework. Cogeneration

facilities placed online before ERCOT market deregulation were planned and financed based on a


                                                 8
 different regulatory structure—a structure that was strongly summer peak based, which was

continued from market open until the present time. Applying a materially different 12CP exposure

to those existing facilities—particularly during their customary maintenance months—would

create a significant retrospective change to the economics of facilities that were designed to

efficiently self-supply industrial load, and to only take maintenance outages when they were not

harmful to the grid or other customers. The Commission should avoid creating disincentives for

the continued operation, maintenance, and reinvestment in legacy cogeneration facilities.

Relatedly, the Commission should make clear that legacy cogeneration facilities are not to be

treated the same as new large load interconnections (such as data centers) or other primarily grid-

dependent loads. An industrial facility that is served by highly reliable, substantially self-

supplying cogeneration has materially different operational characteristics, system impacts, and

investment history than a new large load customer seeking interconnection to the ERCOT grid.

    B. Alternatively, if the Commission shifts fully to a 12CP allocation methodology without
       any grandfathering, it should establish a targeted “safe harbor” exemption to avoid
       penalizing legacy cogeneration facilities for taking maintenance outages during the
       spring and fall.
        If the Commission ultimately adopts a 12CP transmission cost allocation methodology, it

should exclude the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December) from the

CP allocation calculation for legacy cogeneration facilities’ loads. Under this approach, legacy

cogeneration facilities would remain subject to the adopted CP methodology during the remainder

of the year, and would therefore retain strong cost incentives to keep their cogeneration online and

fully operational when demand on the ERCOT grid is at its highest. This targeted exemption

would balance the Commission’s broader policy objectives with the operational realities of legacy,

high-reliability industrial cogeneration facilities.




                                                   9
        A spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December) safe harbor is

appropriate because those seasons are customary and operationally appropriate periods for planned

cogeneration maintenance. Cogeneration facilities commonly schedule planned maintenance

outages during the lower-demand spring and fall, when that maintenance can be performed with

comparatively less impact on system reliability and plant operations. Expanding CP measurement

to all twelve months of the year would penalize those established maintenance practices, even

though they support long-term generation reliability. A targeted safe harbor in the spring and fall,

by contrast, would preserve the operational flexibility necessary for qualifying facilities to conduct

planned outages and return their cogeneration units to service in reliable condition ahead of higher-

demand periods.

       For the same reasons, the proposed exemption would support reliability on the ERCOT

grid, not undermine it. Properly maintained onsite cogeneration reduces co-located loads’ reliance

on the ERCOT transmission system and provides dependable, dispatchable electricity to both the

integrated industrial load and the broader ERCOT grid. Penalizing scheduled maintenance through

12CP allocation may incentivize the postponement of necessary maintenance or other

economically inefficient operating decisions, and, under extreme circumstances, could threaten the

continued economic viability of legacy cogeneration facilities (both generation and load)—

potentially resulting in the permanent closure of those facilities. Moreover, as discussed above,

incentivizing demand reductions during the spring and fall provides no corresponding system

benefit, and may actually harm reliability by causing load reductions during periods when the

system lacks sufficient inertia on the supply side.        A targeted safe harbor to account for

cogeneration maintenance in the spring and fall thus recognizes that maintaining high-reliability

cogeneration resources benefits both the exempted customer and the broader ERCOT system.


                                                 10
     C. Recommended eligibility criteria for legacy cogeneration facilities to qualify for 4CP
       grandfathering or a spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November,
       December) “safe harbor.”
        As discussed above, if the Commission chooses to depart from its traditional 4CP

transmission cost allocation methodology, it should create an exemption for legacy cogeneration

facilities that either (1) continues allocating transmission costs to those facilities based on a 4CP

methodology or (2) exempts those facilities from incurring transmission charges related to their

demand during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December).

        Regardless of which path the Commission takes to insulate legacy cogeneration facilities

from the impact of changing its approach to transmission cost allocation, OxyChem believes the

Commission could create a narrow, administrable exemption by limiting eligibility to facilities

that satisfy the following criteria:

        •   Cogeneration requirement: To qualify for an exemption, an industrial load must

            include onsite cogeneration resources that provide dispatchable electric generation and

            useful thermal energy to an industrial facility or steam host.

                o Justification: This requirement will ensure that eligible customers are part of

                    an integrated qualifying cogeneration facility that has the operational

                    characteristics that justify an exemption from a 12CP transmission cost

                    allocation construct, as discussed above.

        •   Legacy-resource requirement: The cogeneration resource must have been

            commercially operational on or before January 1, 2002.

                o Justification: This requirement will limit the exemption to the relatively small

                    number of legacy facilities that were planned and financed prior to ERCOT

                    market deregulation. OxyChem believes this limitation is reasonable because


                                                 11
                    the pre-2002 regulatory framework was markedly different, such that the

                   economics of those legacy facilities may not be able to withstand an

                   unmitigated shift to 12CP transmission cost allocation.

   D. Recommended provisions for administering a qualifying cogeneration exemption.
       It would be relatively straightforward to administer either of OxyChem’s proposals.

Legacy cogeneration facilities would be given an opportunity to provide documentation to the

applicable Transmission and Distribution Utility (TDU) demonstrating that they satisfy the

eligibility requirements laid out above. Once eligibility is established, the allocation of costs (and

ultimate billing to each eligible customer) will be based either on 4CP (under the grandfathering

approach), or have the spring and fall months (March, April, May and October, November,

December) excluded from the allocation of costs to the applicable TDU (and ultimately, to the

eligible end-use customer), as required under the safe harbor proposal. OxyChem is proposing

rule language to accomplish this.


                                      III.    CONCLUSION

       OxyChem appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments and looks forward to

working with the Commission and other stakeholders as this project moves forward.




                                                 12

     EXECUTIVE SUMMARY TO OXYCHEM’S COMMENTS TO PROPOSED
          AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 AND §25.193 AND NEW §25.252

 •   OxyChem operates seven large chemical plants across the ERCOT region that collectively
     employ over 1,500 Texans. Its two largest Texas plants are co-located and operationally
     integrated with dispatchable qualifying cogeneration units that supply electricity and steam
     to integrated manufacturing operations, reduce demand on the ERCOT grid, and support
     system reliability and resource adequacy. These benefits are not confined to OxyChem’s
     co-located host load. Legacy cogeneration facilities reduce net demand on the shared
     transmission system, help defer or avoid costly transmission investment that would
     otherwise be recovered from all ratepayers, and provide dependable capacity when it is
     most valuable to system reliability—advantages that flow through to all customer classes.
 •   The Commission should retain the existing 4CP transmission cost allocation methodology.
     The 4CP construct is rooted in cost causation and it aligns customers’ incentives with the
     needs of the ERCOT grid, including strong incentives to keep cogeneration fully
     operational during the summer peaks and to schedule maintenance in the spring and fall
     when demand is at its lowest. These incentives benefit the entire ERCOT system. Fully
     operational, high-reliability cogeneration lowers the aggregate capacity and transmission
     investment needed to serve the grid, which helps hold down costs for all customers.
 •   A 12CP methodology would penalize legacy cogeneration facilities for performing
     operationally prudent maintenance during low-demand spring and fall months, shift costs
     onto high load factor industrial customers without any cost-causative rationale, weaken
     incentives that support grid reliability, and could threaten the continued economic viability
     of legacy cogeneration facilities. If that occurs, more of that load would be served directly
     by the ERCOT grid, increasing the need for new generation and transmission investment
     and heightening system-wide scarcity pricing exposure—costs that are ultimately borne by
     all rate classes, including residential customers, not just legacy cogeneration facilities.
 •   If the Commission departs from the 4CP methodology, it should grandfather legacy
     cogeneration facilities and continue to allocate transmission costs to the loads at those sites
     based on their usage during ERCOT’s summer 4CP. Alternatively, the Commission should
     at a minimum adopt a targeted “safe harbor” that excludes the spring (March, April, May)
     and fall (October, November, December) from the CP allocation calculation for legacy
     cogeneration facilities, so those facilities are not assigned transmission costs for taking
     prudent maintenance outages when the transmission system has ample capacity.
 •   Either exemption would be limited to industrial loads that (1) include onsite cogeneration
     resources providing dispatchable electric generation and useful thermal energy to an
     industrial facility or steam host, and (2) have cogeneration that was commercially
     operational on or before January 1, 2002.

                     ATTACHMENT TO OXYCHEM’S COMMENTS


        PROPOSED RULE LANGUAGE TO IMPLEMENT OXYCHEM’S
   RECOMMENDED EXCEPTIONS FOR LEGACY COGENERATION FACILITIES



Explanatory Note

As discussed in OxyChem’s comments, if the Commission departs from its traditional 4CP
transmission cost allocation methodology, it should create a narrow, administrable exemption for
legacy industrial loads that are co-located with qualifying cogeneration (collectively “legacy
cogeneration facilities”). OxyChem is providing two alternative, self-contained versions of
proposed rule language. Version 1 implements OxyChem’s primary recommendation by allowing
legacy cogeneration facilities to continue incurring transmission charges based on a 4CP
methodology even if the Commission otherwise adopts a 12CP methodology. Version 2
implements OxyChem’s alternative recommendation by exempting legacy cogeneration facilities
from incurring transmission charges based on their demand during the spring and fall, while
leaving those facilities subject to the Commission’s adopted CP methodology during the remainder
of the year.

Each version is drafted as a set of modifications/additions to the Commission’s proposed §25.192
(relating to Transmission Service Rates), together with conforming treatment under §25.193
(relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery Factor (TCRF)). The
subsection headings (x) and (y) are intended as placeholders for new subsection names.

VERSION 1: RETENTION OF 4CP ALLOCATION FOR LEGACY COGENERATION
                            FACILITIES

A. Modification to proposed § 25.192(d)(1)

(d). . . (1)   A TSP’s network transmission service rate must be calculated as its commission-
approved transmission cost of service divided by the ERCOT 12CP load sum of: (i) the ERCOT
12CP load, excluding any 12CP load attributable to legacy cogeneration facilities, as defined in
subsection (x) of this section; and (ii) the aggregate coincident peak load of all legacy
cogeneration facilities in the ERCOT region in the months of June, July, August, and September.
In a proceeding to establish network transmission service rates under this section, the ERCOT
12CP load value to be used in calculating a TSP’s rate, inclusive of any modifications required

                                               2
 by this section, must be the most recently approved ERCOT 12CP load in effect prior to the date
of approval of the TSP’s new network transmission service rate in the proceeding. The rate
approved may not exceed the noticed rate under any circumstance.

B. Modification to proposed § 25.192(f)(1)

(f)(1) 12CP. No later than December 1 of each year, ERCOT must determine and file with the
commission the current year’s DSP 12CP load for each DSP, based on the ERCOT 12CP
intervals ending the immediately preceding September, inclusive of any modifications required
by this section. ERCOT must also include in this filing the ERCOT 12CP load for the current
year. For purposes of administering subsection (x) of this section, ERCOT must also file with the
commission an accounting of the portion of the ERCOT 12CP load and the DSP 12CP load for
each DSP that is attributable to demand from legacy cogeneration facilities. The measurement of
the ERCOT system monthly peak demand for purposes of determining the ERCOT 12CP
intervals and the determination of the DSP demand values that coincide with the ERCOT 12CP
intervals must be in accordance with ERCOT protocols. The commission may approve changes
to DSP 12CP values and the ERCOT 12CP value at any time.

C. New § 25.192(x)

(x) Exemption for legacy cogeneration facilities. Notwithstanding any other provision of this
      section, each TSP’s network transmission service rate shall be adjusted to account for
      retaining the 4CP allocation methodology for legacy cogeneration facilities in accordance
      with this subsection, including adjusting the billing units under subsection (f). 2
        (1)    Certification criteria. The DSP providing service to a customer that has a
                cogeneration facility must certify a facility as a legacy cogeneration facility if the
                facility demonstrates that:
                 (A)    the facility includes one or more co-located, dispatchable cogeneration
                          resources that provide electric generation and useful thermal energy to an
                          integrated industrial facility;
                 (B) those cogeneration resources were commercially operational on or before
                       January 1, 2002.
        (2) Notice of Material Change. A legacy cogeneration facility must promptly notify the
              applicable DSP if it no longer complies with the criteria in paragraph (1)(A) of this
              subsection. A facility that no longer satisfies the criteria in paragraph (1)(A) of this
              subsection ceases to be a legacy cogeneration facility beginning with the next
              annual determination of transmission rates and charges under this section.
        (3) Calculation of rates and charges.
                 (A)    Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, a TSP’s network
                         transmission service rate must be calculated as its commission-approved
                         transmission cost of service divided by the sum of: (i) the ERCOT 12CP

                        load, excluding any 12CP load attributable to legacy cogeneration facilities;
                       and (ii) the aggregate coincident peak load of all legacy cogeneration
                       facilities in the ERCOT region in the months of June, July, August, and
                       September.
               (B) The monthly network transmission service charge to be paid by each DSP is
                     the product of the TSP’s monthly rate and the sum of: (i) the DSP’s

                     service area during the coincident peaks in the months of June, July, August,

D. New § 25.193(y)

(x) Exemption for legacy cogeneration facilities. Notwithstanding any other provision of this
      section, the transmission billing demand for a legacy cogeneration facility, as defined in
      § 25.192(x) of this title, is that facility’s billing demand during the summer 4CP rather than
      the ERCOT 12CP. Each DSP must charge to a legacy cogeneration facility only those
      transmission charges attributable to that facility’s demand during the four coincident peaks
      in the months of June, July, August, and September.
E. Necessary revision to definition of “ALLOC” in the TCRF formula located in draft
§ 25.193(c):

       •   “ALLOC is the most recent class allocator based on class demands coincident with the
           most recent ERCOT 12CP intervals, as defined in §25.192 of this title (relating to
           Transmission Service Rates), excluding demand from legacy cogeneration facilities
           that occurs during of the coincident peaks in January, February, March, April, May,
           October, November, and December, adjusted for line losses based upon the most recent
           available line loss values used to calculate rates in the DSP’s most recently approved
           comprehensive base rate proceeding before the commission or those published by
           ERCOT, and further adjusted to include each large load customer’s large load
           minimum billing demands in lieu of the large load customer’s actual 12CP demand
           where that customer’s 12CP demand is less than that customer’s large load minimum
           billing demand, unless otherwise ordered by the commission; and…”

           VERSION 2: SPRING AND FALL “SAFE HARBOR” FOR LEGACY
                         COGENERATION FACILITIES

                                      I.    INTRODUCTION

       Occidental Chemical Corporation (OxyChem) appreciates the opportunity to submit these

comments to express its serious concerns with the proposed changes to the Commission' s

transmission cost allocation policies and to recommend that the Commission adopt narrow,

specific exceptions to any new cost allocation methodology to account for the operational and

business realities that face legacy industrial sites that are co-located with dispatchable qualifying

cogeneration facilities (collectively, "legacy cogeneration facilities").       Specifically, if the

Commission departs from its existing 4CP transmission cost allocation methodology, it should

grandfather legacy cogeneration facilities from that change and continue to allocate transmission

charges to the loads at those sites based on their usage during ERCOT' s summer 4CP.

Alternatively, if the Commission wishes to adopt a more targeted exemption, it should at least

ensure that legacy cogeneration facilities are not assigned transmission costs based on their usage

during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December), when the

transmission system has ample capacity and cogeneration is generally taken offline for prudent

preventative maintenance. Special consideration is warranted for legacy cogeneration facilities

like OxyChem's, which were financed and constructed decades ago under prior regulatory

constructs that focused transmission cost allocation on usage during the summer peaks.            As

described below, a 12CP system would disproportionately penalize legacy cogeneration facilities



                                                  1
 for performing operationally prudent maintenance during the spring and fall, would diminish

economic incentives to prioritize the reliable operation of their cogeneration, and could severely

impact their continued economic viability, to the detriment of all rate classes, including

residentials, and the ERCOT grid overall.

         OxyChem operates seven large chemical plants across the ERCOT region that, as of July

2026 , collectively employ over 1 , 500 Texans . 1 Reliable and cost- effective electricity is a critical

operational input to OxyChem's manufacturing operations and a key factor influencing the global

competitiveness and long-term viability of its facilities. At OxyChem's two largest Texas plants,

electricity is a critical raw material and represents one ofthe largest components of operating costs.

Those two facilities are co-located and operationally integrated with cogeneration units that

provide, steam, waste heat, and electricity for integrated manufacturing operations. Importantly,

because OxyChem's cogeneration provides essential power and steam to its manufacturing plants,

OxyChem is strongly incentivized to keep those generators running around the clock, with a focus

on high reliability, especially at times when generation reserves are low on the grid and procuring

replacement power would be especially expensive. This cogeneration structure not only benefits

OxyChem by allowing it to meet a significant share of its manufacturing plants' electricity needs

throughout the year, it also results in operational efficiencies that reduce demand on the grid.

Additionally, the reliability and availability of OxyChem' s thermal, dispatchable cogeneration also

directly contributes to system stability and resource adequacy because those sites have the

flexibility to reduce their co-located load in order to increase exports, which provides additional

dispatchable capacity on the grid at critical times.



         1 As of July 2026, OxyChem's seven manufacturing facilities employ 1,049 direct employees and 482
contractors.  Those numbers do not include corporate positions that support the manufacturing plants, nor the
additional contractors who are employed on an ad hoc basis for specific projects or plant turnarounds.

                                                     2
         OxyChem strongly supports retaining ERCOT's current four summer coincident peak

(4CP) allocation methodology. The Commission's current 4CP system is appropriately rooted in

cost causation principles because it assigns transmission costs to customers based on their

contribution to ERCOT' s system peaks, and the need to reliably serve peak demand is what

actually drives the need for most new transmission investment.              Further, 4CP allocation

appropriately aligns customers' incentives with the needs of the ERCOT grid. This is especially

true of industrial facilities, like OxyChem's largest facilities, that are integrated with cogeneration

and have a much different impact on the ERCOT grid than loads that are entirely served from the

ERCOT transmission system.         The Commission' s current transmission cost allocation rules

provide legacy cogeneration facilities with strong price signals to ensure that cogeneration units

are operating at their full capacity across each of the 4CPs, because that will mitigate the coincident

peak transmission charges that the co-located loads are assigned in the coming year. Even outside

of the 4CP, OxyChem keeps its cogeneration units up and running across most hours of the year,

which minimizes its net demand on the ERCOT system across far more thanjust the peak intervals.

That said, like any generation facilities, OxyChem's cogeneration units cannot stay online

indefinitely. Under the current transmission cost allocation system, OxyChem is appropriately

incentivized to time its cogeneration maintenance activities (and other operational events that

result in more of OxyChem' s demand being placed on the grid) during the spring (March, April,

May) and fall (October, November, December) when demand on the ERCOT grid is at its lowest.

From a policy perspective, it makes sense to encourage planned generation maintenance in the

spring and fall because that results in some or all of the co-located load being served by the grid

at times when additional demand does not contribute to ERCOT's annual system peak or cause

ERCOT utilities to incur additional costs to expand the transmission system.



                                                  3
        In contrast, under a 12CP system, customers would incur transmission charges based on

their demand during the peak interval in every month, regardless of whether that peak interval has

any bearing on the need for more transmission. Shifting to a 12CP transmission cost allocation

scheme would interfere with customers' incentives to minimize their demand on the ERCOT grid

across the most critical intervals for both reliability and system costs. Providing customers with

signals to manage their usage during low-demand months does not create any reliability benefits

and does not conform with cost-causation principles. Instead, 12CP allocation simply serves to

shift costs onto higher load factor industrial customers, including some, like OxyChem, whose

contributions to ERCOT's monthly CPs are at their greatest when overall demand on the system

is at its lowest, something the Commission should seek to protect and actively encourage.

Specifically, a 12CP system would unfairly penalize facilities like OxyChem's by saddling them

with transmission charges for placing additional demand on the grid when they engage in

necessary and operationally prudent cogeneration maintenance, even if they efficiently arrange

their maintenance intervals in low-demand months when the outages will have the least possible

impact on the broader grid.

       However, in the event the Commission decides to shift transmission cost allocation in

ERCOT to a 12CP system, OxyChem strongly recommends that the Commission create an

exemption that will grandfather and allow a small set of legacy cogeneration facilities to continue

to be billed under the current 4CP construct.       As discussed above, the current 4CP system

appropriately incentivizes reductions in grid usage during the four summer peaks, which has

reliability benefits and diminishes the need for future transmission investment. Additionally,

retaining a 4CP methodology for a limited set of legacy cogeneration facilities will preserve those

facilities' strong financial incentives to ensure that their cogeneration is online and fully


                                                4
 operational during ERCOT' s highest system peaks so that it can offset the demand of the co-

located load and provide any excess capacity onto the ERCOT grid, as well as those sites'

incentives to schedule cogeneration maintenance during the spring and fall (March-May and

October-December) when the reliability ofthe ERCOT grid is not in question, and when the drivers

for new transmission investment are not present. In contrast, incentivizing demand reductions

during off-peak months has no corresponding system benefit, and may actually harm reliability by

causing load reductions when the system lacks sufficient inertia on the supply side. Further,

retaining the current 4CP allocation methodology will preserve the economics of legacy

cogeneration facilities, many of which were financed and built under prior regulatory constructs,

including those that pre-date market open, which all had a strong 4CP element to reflect the

realities ofthe ERCOT system. Moving away from this long-standing policy could jeopardize the

ability of legacy cogeneration facilities (not just OxyChem' s, but also those of other industrial

companies engaged in energy intensive industries) to maintain profitability and continue operating

at their current scale. This is because legacy cogeneration facilities that typically only use the

ERCOT transmission system as a backup source of supply would be forced to begin paying

significant transmission charges-not because of any operational characteri sues that put strain on

the ERCOT grid or cause the need for new transmission investment, but simply because they chose

to engage in prudent and necessary cogeneration maintenance practices that not only benefit their

operators, but the broader ERCOT grid. Such a result would be exceedingly poor public policy.

       Alternatively, ifthe Commission wishes to apply an updated allocation methodology (such

as 12CP) to legacy cogeneration facilities, the Commission should create a targeted exemption

process that would at least allow those facilities to avoid incurring transmission charges based on

their net demand during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December).



                                                5
 Such an exemption or "safe harbor" would encourage legacy cogeneration facilities to engage in

operationally prudent generation maintenance at times when taking their generation offline poses

the least possible reliability risk and least cost impact, while still incentivizing them to keep that

generation online and fully operational to offset their exposure to transmission charges during the

remainder of the year.    In contrast, if those facilities are subjected to a 12CP cost allocation

methodology without any exemption, that would expose them to significant transmission cost

disincentives on prudently maintaining and efficiently operating legacy cogeneration facilities

would hurt ratepayers across a// customer classes, including residential customers, by increasing

       As described below, if the Commission chooses to depart from its traditional 4CP

facilities. Notably, while OxyChem believes that such an exemption is justified based on the

                                 II.   GENERAL COMMENTS

   A. The Commission should retain the existing 4CP transmission cost allocation
      methodology, either generally across ERCOT or specifically for legacy cogeneration
       facilities.
       As explained above, the Commission' s current 4CP transmission cost allocation

methodology is appropriately rooted in cost causation principles and should be retained. The need

to reliably serve peak demand is what actually drives the need for new transmission investment,

and the 4CP construct assigns transmission costs to customers based on their contributions to the

four system peaks that occur during the summer months, when overall demand on the ERCOT

grid is at its highest. Just as importantly, the current methodology aligns customers' incentives

with the needs of the ERCOT grid. Because customers can reduce their transmission charges by

minimizing their demand during the 4CP intervals, the current system rewards behavior-like

keeping co-located cogeneration online and fully operational across the summer peaks-that

provides real reliability benefits and diminishes the need for future transmission investment. In

other words, reductions in grid usage during the four summer peaks have an offsetting benefit to

the grid, which is precisely the type of cost-causative relationship that should underlie any

transmission cost allocation methodology.

       However, if the Commission decides to abandon the 4CP system, given the unique

characteristics of legacy cogeneration facilities like OxyChem's, it would be prudent and fair for

the Commission to grandfather those facilities and allow them to continue to be billed based on

the 4CP methodology. At industrial cogeneration sites, industrial electrical load, steam demand,

process operations, and cogeneration output are operationally interconnected. Generation dispatch

decisions at those sites must prioritize safe, reliable, and efficient operation of continuous

industrial processes, including steam balance, process heat requirements, equipment constraints,

emissions compliance, and worker safety.      Unlike stand-alone loads, cogeneration facilities

                                                7
 generally cannot treat electric load reduction as a simple economic response without potentially

disrupting production, process safety, product quality, contractual commitments, or steam system

reliability. As such, load curtailment solely to mitigate coincident peak transmission charges is

not a primary operational objective for legacy cogeneration facilities. The Commission should

avoid a cost allocation structure that encourages those facilities to make operational decisions

based primarily on poor transmission billing signals rather than safe, reliable, efficient, and

environmentally responsible integrated operations.

        These operational realities also demonstrate why a 12CP methodology would be

particularly inappropriate for legacy cogeneration facilities. A methodology based on a broader

set of monthly system peaks would subject those facilities to transmission cost exposure during

periods when operationally prudent generation maintenance or process conditions limit their

ability to optimize their net load.   And, during the spring and fall, managing usage during

ERCOT's monthly peak intervals provides no offsetting benefit to the grid-it simply shifts costs

to industrial customers without any corresponding cost-causative rationale.         In contrast, as

discussed above, reducing demand on the grid during the four summer peak intervals does provide

an offsetting benefit, because those are the intervals that drive the need for new transmission

investment and present the greatest risk to the reliability of the ERCOT grid. Further, diluting the

impact of the summer 4CP will decrease legacy cogeneration facilities' incentives to ensure that

their thermal, dispatchable generation is maximally available at the most critical times for grid

stability and reliability.

        Finally, the Commission should recognize that legacy cogeneration facilities were

developed under a materially different regulatory and cost allocation framework. Cogeneration

facilities placed online before ERCOT market deregulation were planned and financed based on a


                                                 8
 different regulatory structure-a structure that was strongly summer peak based, which was

continued from market open until the present time. Applying a materially different 12CP exposure

to those existing facilities-particularly during their customary maintenance months-would

create a significant retrospective change to the economics of facilities that were designed to

efficiently self-supply industrial load, and to only take maintenance outages when they were not

harmful to the grid or other customers. The Commission should avoid creating disincentives for

the continued operation, maintenance, and reinvestment in legacy cogeneration facilities.

Relatedly, the Commission should make clear that legacy cogeneration facilities are not to be

treated the same as new large load interconnections (such as data centers) or other primarily grid-

dependent loads.     An industrial facility that is served by highly reliable, substantially self-

supplying cogeneration has materially different operational characteristics, system impacts, and

investment history than a new large load customer seeking interconnection to the ERCOT grid.


    B. Alternatively, if the Commission shifts fully to a 12CP allocation methodology without
       any grandfathering, it should establish a targeted "safe harbor" exemption to avoid
       penalizing legacy cogeneration facilities for taking maintenance outages during the
       spring and fall.
        If the Commission ultimately adopts a 12CP transmission cost allocation methodology, it

should exclude the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December) from the

CP allocation calculation for legacy cogeneration facilities' loads. Under this approach, legacy

cogeneration facilities would remain subj ect to the adopted CP methodology during the remainder

of the year, and would therefore retain strong cost incentives to keep their cogeneration online and

fully operational when demand on the ERCOT grid is at its highest. This targeted exemption

would balance the Commission' s broader policy objectives with the operational realities of legacy,

high-reliability industrial cogeneration facilities.




                                                   9
        A spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December) safe harbor is

appropriate because those seasons are customary and operationally appropriate periods for planned

cogeneration maintenance.      Cogeneration facilities commonly schedule planned maintenance

outages during the lower-demand spring and fall, when that maintenance can be performed with

comparatively less impact on system reliability and plant operations. Expanding CP measurement

to all twelve months of the year would penalize those established maintenance practices, even

though they support long-term generation reliability. A targeted safe harbor in the spring and fall,

by contrast, would preserve the operational flexibility necessary for qualifying facilities to conduct

planned outages and return their cogeneration units to service in reliable condition ahead ofhigher-

demand periods.

       For the same reasons, the proposed exemption would support reliability on the ERCOT

grid, not undermine it. Properly maintained onsite cogeneration reduces co-located loads' reliance

on the ERCOT transmission system and provides dependable, dispatchable electricity to both the

integrated industrial load and the broader ERCOT grid. Penalizing scheduled maintenance through

12CP allocation may incentivize the postponement of necessary maintenance or other

economically inefficient operating decisions, and, under extreme circumstances, could threaten the

continued economic viability of legacy cogeneration facilities (both generation and load)-

potentially resulting in the permanent closure of those facilities. Moreover, as discussed above,

incentivizing demand reductions during the spring and fall provides no corresponding system

benefit, and may actually harm reliability by causing load reductions during periods when the

system lacks sufficient inertia on the supply side.        A targeted safe harbor to account for

cogeneration maintenance in the spring and fall thus recognizes that maintaining high-reliability

cogeneration resources benefits both the exempted customer and the broader ERCOT system.



                                                  10
     C. Recommended eligibility criteria for legacy cogeneration facilities to qualify for 4CP
       grandfathering or a spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November,
       December) "safe harbor."
        As discussed above, if the Commission chooses to depart from its traditional 4CP

transmission cost allocation methodology, it should create an exemption for legacy cogeneration

facilities that either (1) continues allocating transmission costs to those facilities based on a 4CP

methodology or (2) exempts those facilities from incurring transmission charges related to their

demand during the spring (March, April, May) and fall (October, November, December).

        Regardless of which path the Commission takes to insulate legacy cogeneration facilities

from the impact of changing its approach to transmission cost allocation, OxyChem believes the

Commission could create a narrow, administrable exemption by limiting eligibility to facilities

that satisfy the following criteria:

        •   Cogeneration requirement:       To qualify for an exemption, an industrial load must

            include onsite cogeneration resources that provide dispatchable electric generation and

            useful thermal energy to an industrial facility or steam host.

                o   Justification: This requirement will ensure that eligible customers are part of

                    an integrated qualifying cogeneration facility that has the operational

                    characteristics that justify an exemption from a 12CP transmission cost

                    allocation construct, as discussed above.

        •   Legacy-resource      requirement:    The   cogeneration resource must have been

            commercially operational on or before January 1, 2002.

                o   Justification: This requirement willlimit the exemption to the relatively small

                    number of legacy facilities that were planned and financed prior to ERCOT

                    market deregulation. OxyChem believes this limitation is reasonable because


                                                  11
                    the pre-2002 regulatory framework was markedly different, such that the

                   economics of those legacy facilities may not be able to withstand an

                   unmitigated shift to 12CP transmission cost allocation.

   D. Recommended provisions for administering a qualifying cogeneration exemption.
       It would be relatively straightforward to administer either of OxyChem's proposals.

Legacy cogeneration facilities would be given an opportunity to provide documentation to the

applicable Transmission and Distribution Utility (TDU) demonstrating that they satisfy the

eligibility requirements laid out above. Once eligibility is established, the allocation of costs (and

ultimate billing to each eligible customer) will be based either on 4CP (under the grandfathering

approach), or have the spring and fall months (March, April, May and October, November,

December) excluded from the allocation of costs to the applicable TDU (and ultimately, to the

eligible end-use customer), as required under the safe harbor proposal. OxyChem is proposing

rule language to accomplish this.
